processing: An oolong cultivar made in the partly oxidised, rolled manner; on Wuyi it is finished with a roast like other rock teas.
harvest_season: As with other Fujian oolongs, spring is the usual picking; no specific timing is claimed here.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark strips when made in the Wuyi style.
appearance_liquor: Golden-orange, typical of a lighter roasted Wuyi oolong.
appearance_wet: As with other Wuyi oolongs, open leaves with darkened edges.
taste_profile: No settled tasting description is on record here; it is treated as a fragrant cultivar, so expect a floral lift over a roast base.

brewing.notes: Standard Wuyi oolong brewing; a slightly cooler start protects the aroma if the roast is light.

vintage_note: Usually sold like other Wuyi oolongs, by the year of the spring harvest and after roasting. Ask for the roast level, since a fragrant cultivar can taste very different when roasted hard.
description:
Dan Gui is a Fujian oolong tea cultivar. The same two characters are also the name of orange-flowered osmanthus, so do not assume a bag labelled Dan Gui contains flowers, or that it is scented: here it names the tea plant.

Fujian researchers treat it as a nationally assessed cultivar and have used it as a parent in breeding, crossing it with Ruixiang to obtain the newer cultivar Minggui.

Expect fragrance rather than heavy roast. Brew it hot but start with short steeps, and notice how much of the perfume survives the roast.

When buying, ask about the roast and growing area, and do not read the name as a promise of osmanthus flavour.
history: Dan Gui appears in the work of the Tea Research Institute of the Fujian Academy of Agricultural Sciences, including as a breeding parent. Its parentage and date of release are not established here.
